summary: Sets requirements for NATs that handle TCP, so that applications such as peer-to-peer software and online games can work consistently through them. This is a Best Current Practice, later updated by RFC 7857.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5382 describes how a network address translator should handle TCP connections. Its requirements cover the addresses it assigns, which inbound attempts it allows, and how long it keeps connection state.

questions: how should a nat handle tcp connections
what are the nat requirements for tcp
how long should a nat keep idle tcp connections
subtitle: Requirements that help TCP connections work through network address translators.

tldr.problem: A network address translator can block or alter TCP connection attempts that applications expect to work. This can force peer-to-peer applications to rely on public relays.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5382 sets ten requirements for TCP mapping, filtering, connection setup, timeouts, port assignment, hairpinning and ICMP handling.
tldr.outcome: The requirements aim to make TCP behavior more consistent through NATs. RFC 5382 is a Best Current Practice updated by RFC 7857.

today: RFC 5382 is Best Current Practice 142 and has been updated by RFC 7857. It has not been obsoleted according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 5382 adds TCP requirements to the general NAT requirements in RFC 4787. It applies to traditional NATs and covers TCP behavior that affects NAT traversal.

The motivation is that NATs can prevent applications from starting connections to internal hosts. Peer-to-peer techniques depend on NAT behavior that is common but not guaranteed, so inconsistent behavior can require a public relay.
sections.plainLanguage: This document covers how traditional NATs handle TCP traffic. It aims to make connections through them more predictable for applications.

sections.title: Mappings and TCP Connection Setup
sections.content:
A NAT mapping records how an internal address and port correspond to an external address and port. REQ-1 says a TCP NAT MUST use Endpoint-Independent Mapping: the same internal endpoint gets the same external mapping when it connects to different external endpoints.

REQ-2 says a NAT MUST handle valid TCP packet sequences, including simultaneous-open. In simultaneous-open, both peers send a SYN for the same connection, then each responds to the other with a SYN-ACK.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAT must keep an internal endpoint's external address and port consistent across connections. It must also allow both peers to start the same TCP connection at once.

sections.title: Filtering Inbound Connections
sections.content:
Filtering determines which external hosts may start a connection through an existing mapping. REQ-3 recommends Endpoint-Independent Filtering when application transparency matters most, or Address-Dependent Filtering when stricter filtering matters more. Administrators may be allowed to configure the choice.

REQ-4 says the NAT MUST NOT respond to an unsolicited inbound SYN for at least 6 seconds. If a matching outbound SYN arrives during that interval, it must silently drop the earlier inbound SYN. Otherwise it should send ICMP Port Unreachable unless security policy requires silence.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAT can choose how strictly to filter new inbound connections. It waits at least 6 seconds before answering an unsolicited SYN, giving a matching outbound attempt time to arrive.

sections.title: Connection Timeouts and Application Gateways
sections.content:
A NAT may remove idle connection state when it cannot tell whether the endpoints are still active. If it does, REQ-5 sets minimum idle timeouts: 2 hours 4 minutes for an established connection and 4 minutes for a partially open or closing connection. The values may be configurable.

Application-level gateways can rewrite addresses or ports inside application messages and interfere with NAT traversal. REQ-6 recommends disabling TCP gateways by default, except for FTP because some older clients rely on one.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAT must keep idle TCP state long enough to avoid dropping live connections too soon. Gateways that rewrite application data should usually start disabled.

sections.title: Ports, Hairpinning and ICMP
sections.content:
A TCP NAT MUST NOT assign the same external port mapping to different internal endpoints at the same time. It MUST support hairpinning, which lets two internal endpoints communicate through their external mapped addresses, and it must present the external source address and port.

A NAT that translates TCP SHOULD translate ICMP Destination Unreachable messages. Receiving any ICMP message MUST NOT terminate the TCP connection or its NAT mapping. These requirements include the ICMP messages used by Path MTU Discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: Two internal devices must be able to reach the same external host without sharing one mapping. Devices behind one NAT can also reach each other by their external addresses.

sections.title: Security Trade-Offs and Status
sections.content:
Filtering involves a trade-off: stricter filtering limits inbound connections, while looser filtering supports more applications. The RFC explains that Endpoint-Independent Filtering requires an attacker to guess an active mapping's address and port; Address-Dependent Filtering also requires guessing the external address.

NATs that change TCP sequence numbers must handle Selective Acknowledgment correctly. NATs that use TCP flags to update state must also handle packets that fall outside the expected sequence window.
sections.plainLanguage: Stricter filtering can reduce unwanted access but can also block connection attempts. The RFC also calls for care when a NAT changes TCP sequence numbers or tracks TCP state.
